claims.text: What the image looks like Transition point in dilated SB; whirl/whirlpool sign → closed-loop SBO / volvulus → ischemia risk
claims.quote: Transition point in dilated SB; whirl/whirlpool sign Closed-loop SBO / volvulus → ischemia risk

claims.text: Buzzword: whirl / whirlpool sign on CT abdomen = volvulus / mesenteric twist
claims.quote: Whirl / whirlpool sign CT abdomen Volvulus / mesenteric twist

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Example CT of SBO: dilated small bowel filled with air and fluid, with collapsed cecum and sigmoid colon; a transition point cannot always be seen, but dilated proximal and collapsed distal bowel are highly suggestive
claims.quote: In this CT scan, the small bowel is dilated and filled with air and fluid. Oral contrast is seen in some of the loops but has not traveled down to the distal small bowel. Note the collapsed cecum and sigmoid colon (arrows). A specific point of obstruction (transition point) cannot always be seen on CT, but the dilated proximal bowel and collapsed distal bowel are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.

claims.text: Abdominal CT is being used more often in suspected small-bowel obstruction
claims.quote: Abdominal CT is being used more often in suspected small-bowel obstruction.

claims.text: Only laparotomy can definitively diagnose strangulation; elevated WBC and acidosis may indicate it has already occurred, but may be absent
claims.quote: Although only laparotomy can definitively diagnose strangulation, careful serial clinical examination may provide early warning. Elevated white blood cells and acidosis may indicate that strangulation has already occurred, but these signs may be absent if the venous outflow from the strangulated loop of bowel is decreased.

claims.text: Causes Strangulating obstruction = obstruction with compromised blood flow (nearly 25% of SBOs), usually with hernia, volvulus or intussusception
claims.quote: Strangulating obstruction is obstruction with compromised blood flow; it occurs in nearly 25% of patients with small-bowel obstruction (1). It is usually associated with hernia, volvulus, and intussusception.

claims.text: It can progress to infarction and gangrene in as little as 6 hours: venous obstruction first, then arterial occlusion
claims.quote: Strangulating obstruction can progress to infarction and gangrene in as little as 6 hours. Venous obstruction occurs first, followed by arterial occlusion, resulting in rapid ischemia of the bowel wall.

claims.text: Volvulus = twisting of bowel on its mesentery
claims.quote: Other general causes are diverticulitis, foreign bodies (including gallstones), volvulus (twisting of bowel on its mesentery), intussusception (telescoping of one segment of bowel into another), and fecal impaction.

claims.text: Symptoms SBO: periumbilical or epigastric cramps, vomiting and (if complete) obstipation; severe, steady pain suggests strangulation
claims.quote: Obstruction of the small bowel causes symptoms shortly after onset: abdominal cramps centered around the umbilicus or in the epigastrium, vomiting, and—in patients with complete obstruction—obstipation. Patients with partial obstruction may develop diarrhea. Severe, steady pain suggests that strangulation has occurred.

claims.text: With infarction the abdomen becomes tender with a silent abdomen or minimal peristalsis; shock and oliguria indicate late simple obstruction or strangulation
claims.quote: With infarction, the abdomen becomes tender and auscultation reveals a silent abdomen or minimal peristalsis. Shock and oliguria are serious signs that indicate either late simple obstruction or strangulation.

claims.text: Volvulus often has an abrupt onset; pain is continuous, sometimes with superimposed colicky waves
claims.quote: Volvulus often has an abrupt onset. Pain is continuous, sometimes with superimposed waves of colicky pain.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: emergent surgery
Complete SBO is preferentially treated with early laparotomy (can be delayed 2 or 3 hours to improve fluid status in a very ill, dehydrated patient)
claims.quote: Complete obstruction of the small bowel is preferentially treated with early laparotomy, although surgery can be delayed 2 or 3 hours to improve fluid status and urine output in a very ill, dehydrated patient.

claims.text: If ischemia or infarction is suspected: antibiotics (eg, cefotetan or cefoxitin) before operative exploration
claims.quote: If bowel ischemia or infarction is suspected, antibiotics should be given (eg, a third-generation cephalosporin, such as cefotetan or cefoxitin) before operative exploration.
